Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

let BadHashes = dynamic(["D511B77459673EC42163F19E300FF1D233B6C39F", "59A8553A4F8130F576AB234E0B220BE4D4DA0E98", "9CA1A5C7F79882DB913534C1E62B26BCDCB9F6DD", "A8E2BBBFCB86500322D2367744FA12755AB0C165", "F74F1FEB62B662CDA489FDB2453727824E55ACB9", "F8F8209987CA7F139DE6A62F9E6EE21BD2AE93A9", "19A69F856EFA811C376F68E4FEB0997B4724F8BD", "490194E9BB5128ECA8693AD9E610891C2ED185AF", "51176139B0B2220B802C1578A4994DF68DF5BCD1", "91F042F59BE4BDCB6E5EA21B91DECD731C175B54", "A177ED0BFFEB1EFE1D9D31D72A82EF2625AE646D", "B7B2D2DB544F9EEA74453CDF2B8BEEA58CF07C48", "4AD36AD6C165B5174967020CB1A3358F78D7A283", "57352B3CEEE32216E5AA20BAA848483D7AB5A6FB", "9BC06DF9F932746A05EE728C8B103BD3BA6BF395", "865A1739337D3303B3AB02C5E694C22B79C42B7D", "41CB8CD78B8DB76563E4F972ABE817CEEE9CF9B0", "0037DBB0FEA981D02F6F76DE81EBAEFCB68B7D20", "5D6194BB48FEBB91A10D1462461A012FAFC0918B", "B028E947150764A71DEEF498DE6F8C95ECCCB445"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GitHub to Disable npm Install Scripts by Default to Stop Supply Chain Attacks

The Hacker News
2026-06-11 11 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

GitHub has announced what it said are "breaking changes" coming to npm version 12, one of which turns off install scripts by default to combat software supply chain threats. The changes aim to combat attack techniques that abuse the "npm install" command to trigger the execution of malicious code using npm lifecycle hooks. "Npm install" is used to download and install all the necessary

npm install lifecycle script spawns interpreter or network-fetcher child AIInstallation Medium
Detects suspicious interpreter or downloader children of npm.exe / node.exe during package install — the exact lifecycle-script code-execution surface GitHub is disabling by default in npm 12. The article specifically names preinstall, install, and postinstall scripts (plus implicit node-gyp rebuilds) as the abuse vector. Rationale: Article names preinstall/install/postinstall lifecycle scripts and implicit node-gyp rebuild as the largest npm code-execution surface. Parent-process pivot (npm/node) plus interpreter/downloader child is the canonical shape of recent npm supply-chain payloads (e.g. recent Microsoft GitHub repo worm). Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/github-to-disable-npm-install-scripts.html • https://github.blog/changelog/
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.003 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate native-addon builds where postinstall invokes node-gyp which shells out to cmd.exe and python
  • Developer-owned packages whose preinstall scripts legitimately curl down a binary asset (e.g. puppeteer Chromium, esbuild prebuilt)
  • CI runners where npm install routinely spawns powershell/bash wrappers for cross-platform scripts
  • electron-builder / node-pre-gyp pulling prebuilt binaries on first install
  • Yarn/pnpm wrappers re-invoking npm under the hood and chaining shell calls
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "node-gyp" and ChildImage endswith "\\cmd.exe" and ChildCmd has_any ("python","msbuild")) | where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("puppeteer","playwright","esbuild","node-pre-gyp","electron") and ChildCmd has_any ("https://","download"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree and InitiatingProcessCommandLine; identify the package being installed by checking CWD for package.json/package-lock.json and which dependency owns the running install hook (npm logs at %APPDATA%\npm-cache\_logs). 2) Contain: isolate the host, revoke any npm/GitHub auth tokens present on it (npm token list, gh auth status), and freeze CI runners that share the registry. 3) Hunt: pivot on the package name + version across the fleet, query for the same parent->child shape in the last 30 days, check npm registry advisories and ThreatFox for that package, and inspect ~/.npmrc and project .npmrc for unexpected registry or authToken entries.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","npm ci","npm i ","npm rebuild","node-gyp rebuild")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentImage=InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildImage=FolderPath, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe","\\npm.cmd") or CommandLine has_any ("npm install","npm ci","npm rebuild","node-gyp rebuild")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\cmd.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\curl.exe","\\wget.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\certutil.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: npm install lifecycle script spawns interpreter or network-fetcher child

description: Detects suspicious interpreter or downloader children of npm.exe / node.exe during package install - the lifecycle-script abuse surface GitHub is disabling by default in npm 12.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/github-to-disable-npm-install-scripts.html
author: SOC
date: 2026/06/12
tags:
  - attack.t1059.001
  - attack.t1059.003
  - attack.t1195.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\npm.exe'
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\npm.cmd'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
      - '\rundll32.exe'
      - '\curl.exe'
      - '\bitsadmin.exe'
      - '\certutil.exe'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\npm.exe OR *\\NPM.EXE OR *\\node.exe OR *\\NODE.EXE OR *\\npm.cmd) @Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\\cmd.exe OR *\\CMD.EXE OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\mshta.exe OR *\\curl.exe OR *\\certutil.exe OR *\\bitsadmin.exe OR *\\rundll32.exe)

| ImageFileName=/(powershell|pwsh|cmd|wscript|cscript|mshta|rundll32|curl|wget|bitsadmin|certutil|bash|sh)\.exe$/i

npm install with --allow-git / --allow-remote / --allow-scripts bypass flag AIWeaponization High
Detects explicit use of the new npm 12 allow-list flags (--allow-git, --allow-remote, --allow-scripts) or .npmrc allowScripts=true, which re-open the very code-execution paths GitHub is closing by default. After upgrade, routine use of these flags on developer endpoints is an adversary tell. Rationale: Article calls out --allow-git as the post-v12 opt-in for Git dependencies and --allow-remote for remote URL tarballs, plus the explicit allowScripts default flip. Article also notes the .npmrc-overrides-Git-executable bypass — these flags are the literal strings to grep for. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/github-to-disable-npm-install-scripts.html • https://docs.npmjs.com/cli
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A senior dev who explicitly trusts and runs a Git dependency with --allow-git for one-off prototyping
  • Internal monorepo tooling that legitimately needs --allow-remote for an internal-only tarball mirror
  • CI pipelines that intentionally set allowScripts=true for native-addon builds (e.g. binding.gyp packages)
  • Vendor build steps invoked by Yarn/pnpm that pass the flags through to nested npm calls
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("\\actions-runner\\","\\agent\\","\\TeamCity\\","\\Jenkins\\","\\gitlab-runner\\") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "node-gyp")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the package and registry being installed - check the CWD, package.json, and any --registry argument on the same command line. Pull npm-cli logs from %APPDATA%\npm-cache\_logs. 2) Contain: if the package is from a public/unknown registry, isolate the host and block the registry FQDN at egress; freeze any artifact built by this run. 3) Hunt: search the fleet for the same package name + version with these flags; look for follow-on outbound connections from node.exe / npm.exe to non-corporate IPs within 10 minutes; check .npmrc files org-wide for allowScripts=true or registry overrides.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--allow-git","--allow-remote","--allow-scripts","allowScripts=true","allowScripts = true")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe","\\npm.cmd") or ParentProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("--allow-git","--allow-remote","--allow-scripts","allowScripts=true","allowScripts = true")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: npm install with --allow-git or --allow-remote bypass flag
id: 2b3c4d5e-6f7a-4b8c-9d0e-1f2a3b4c5d6e
description: Detects explicit use of npm 12's allow-list opt-in flags that re-enable Git/remote/script code-execution paths disabled by default after the v12 upgrade.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/github-to-disable-npm-install-scripts.html
author: SOC
date: 2026/06/12
tags:
  - attack.t1562.001
  - attack.t1195.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\npm.exe'
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\npm.cmd'
  selection_flag:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '--allow-git'
      - '--allow-remote'
      - '--allow-scripts'
      - 'allowScripts=true'
  condition: selection_proc and selection_flag
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\npm.exe OR *\\NPM.EXE OR *\\node.exe OR *\\NODE.EXE OR *\\npm.cmd) @CommandLine:(*--allow-git* OR *--allow-remote* OR *--allow-scripts* OR *allowScripts=true*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/^.*\\(npm(\.exe|\.cmd)?|node\.exe)$/i
| regex("(--allow-git|--allow-remote|--allow-scripts|allowScripts\\s*=\\s*true)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd") OR Processes.parent_process_name IN ("npm.exe","node.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process,"(?i)(--allow-git|--allow-remote|--allow-scripts|allowScripts\s*=\s*true)")
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd") OR Processes.parent_process_name IN ("npm.exe","node.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process,"(?i)(--allow-git|--allow-remote|--allow-scripts|allowScripts\s*=\s*true)")
npm install pointing at non-default registry via --registry or config AIDelivery Medium
Hunts npm/node invocations that point at a registry other than npmjs.org or known mirrors — the canonical dependency-confusion / typosquatting setup, and the path an attacker uses once they have a foothold to redirect a developer to a malicious mirror. Pairs with the v12 install-script hardening: an attacker losing scripts will pivot to redirecting the registry itself. Rationale: Article frames npm install as the supply-chain entry point and v12 closes the script-execution path; redirecting the registry is the natural pivot left to attackers. Non-default --registry is a textbook dependency-confusion precursor and is high-signal on developer endpoints (org-approved registries are usually known). Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/github-to-disable-npm-install-scripts.html
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1584.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers using an internal Verdaccio / Artifactory / Nexus / GitHub Packages mirror
  • Open-source contributors pointing at a forked registry for testing a new feature
  • CI runners configured with a corporate mirror that fronts npmjs.org
  • One-off install from a vendor-provided registry during a POC
  • Yarn invocations that pass --registry through to nested npm calls
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("verdaccio","artifactory","nexus","npm.pkg.github.com","jfrog","myget") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("\\actions-runner\\","\\Jenkins\\","\\TeamCity\\","\\agent\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the registry URL from the command line and resolve it - check WHOIS, certificate transparency, and the org's approved-mirror list. Look at the package(s) being installed in the same command. 2) Contain: if the registry is not on the approved list, isolate the host and block the FQDN at egress; quarantine any node_modules built during this run. 3) Hunt: pivot on the registry FQDN across DeviceNetworkEvents for the last 30 days; check whether other developers / CI runners hit the same URL; query for follow-on outbound connections from node.exe within 5 minutes of the install.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--registry" or ProcessCommandLine has "config set registry"
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "registry.npmjs.org"
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "registry.yarnpkg.com"
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "registry.npmmirror.com"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe","\\npm.cmd")
| where CommandLine has "--registry" or CommandLine has "config set registry"
| where CommandLine !has "registry.npmjs.org"
| where CommandLine !has "registry.yarnpkg.com"
| where CommandLine !has "registry.npmmirror.com"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: npm install pointing at non-default registry
id: 3c4d5e6f-7a8b-4c9d-0e1f-2a3b4c5d6e7f
description: Detects npm or node invocations that override the default registry with a non-mainstream URL, a common dependency-confusion setup step.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/github-to-disable-npm-install-scripts.html
author: SOC
date: 2026/06/12
tags:
  - attack.t1195.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\npm.exe'
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\npm.cmd'
  selection_flag:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '--registry'
      - 'config set registry'
  filter_known:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'registry.npmjs.org'
      - 'registry.yarnpkg.com'
      - 'registry.npmmirror.com'
  condition: selection_proc and selection_flag and not filter_known
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\npm.exe OR *\\NPM.EXE OR *\\node.exe OR *\\NODE.EXE OR *\\npm.cmd) @CommandLine:(*--registry* OR *"config set registry"*) -@CommandLine:(*registry.npmjs.org* OR *registry.yarnpkg.com* OR *registry.npmmirror.com*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/^.*\\(npm(\.exe|\.cmd)?|node\.exe)$/i
| regex("(--registry|config\\s+set\\s+registry)", field=CommandLine)
| NOT regex("(registry\\.npmjs\\.org|registry\\.yarnpkg\\.com|registry\\.npmmirror\\.com)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process,"(?i)(--registry|config\s+set\s+registry)") AND NOT match(process,"(?i)(registry\.npmjs\.org|registry\.yarnpkg\.com|registry\.npmmirror\.com)")
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process,"(?i)(--registry|config\s+set\s+registry)") AND NOT match(process,"(?i)(registry\.npmjs\.org|registry\.yarnpkg\.com|registry\.npmmirror\.com)")
npm publish / login / auth-token write from a developer endpoint AIActions on Objectives Medium
Surfaces npm auth and publish CLI activity plus .npmrc credential-file writes on workstations - the precursor to a package-hijack supply-chain attack. Splits the original (broken) single-column lookup into a clean union of DeviceProcessEvents and DeviceFileEvents so neither query references a non-canonical column. Rationale: Article frames npm install as the supply-chain risk, but credential write + publish from a developer endpoint is how a package gets hijacked at source. Hunts for npm publish/login/token CLI flows and .npmrc credential-file writes (which carry _authToken=). Uses canonical Defender columns only - replaces the previous query that referenced a non-existent NpmrcWrites column with a clean union of DeviceProcessEvents and DeviceFileEvents. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/github-to-disable-npm-install-scripts.html • https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v10/configuring-npm/npmrc
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal package authors running npm publish to a private registry as part of normal workflow
  • Onboarding flows that create ~/.npmrc with corporate registry tokens
  • CI agents publishing release artifacts on tag push
  • Developers running npm whoami / npm login after rotating their npm token
  • IDE plugins (VS Code, JetBrains) writing project-local .npmrc files
Suppression filter
| where not (Initiator has_any ("actions-runner","gitlab-runner","TeamCity","Jenkins","agent.exe") and EventKind == "npm_auth_cli")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the user is an authorized package publisher; for .npmrc writes, read the file and look for _authToken=, registry overrides, or always-auth=true on non-corporate hosts. 2) Contain: if unauthorized publish, immediately revoke the npm token (npm token revoke) and the user's npmjs.com session; if a malicious package version was published, contact npm security to deprecate/unpublish and notify downstream consumers. 3) Hunt: pivot on the username across npm registry audit logs for prior publishes; check whether the same .npmrc token appears on other endpoints; look for outbound POSTs to registry.npmjs.org/_token or /-/v1/login from the same host in the last 24h.
let NpmAuth = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm publish","npm login","npm adduser","npm token create","npm token revoke","npm whoami")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, EventKind="npm_auth_cli", Details=ProcessCommandLine, Initiator=InitiatingProcessFileName;
let NpmrcChange = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ ".npmrc"
| where ActionType in~ ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, EventKind="npmrc_write", Details=strcat(FolderPath,"\\",FileName), Initiator=InitiatingProcessFileName;
NpmAuth
| union NpmrcChange
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe","\\npm.cmd")
| where CommandLine has_any ("npm publish","npm login","npm adduser","npm token create","npm token revoke","npm whoami")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, EventKind="npm_auth_cli", Details=CommandLine),
(ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName =~ ".npmrc"
| where EventType in~ ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, Account=ActorUsername, EventKind="npmrc_write", Details=TargetFilePath)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\npm.exe OR *\\NPM.EXE OR *\\node.exe OR *\\NODE.EXE OR *\\npm.cmd) @CommandLine:(*"npm publish"* OR *"npm login"* OR *"npm adduser"* OR *"npm token create"* OR *"npm token revoke"*)) OR (source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\.npmrc OR *\\.NPMRC))
(#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/^.*\\(npm(\.exe|\.cmd)?|node\.exe)$/i
| regex("(npm\\s+(publish|login|adduser|whoami)|npm\\s+token\\s+(create|revoke))", field=CommandLine)) OR (#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\\.npmrc$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, TargetFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process,"(?i)(npm\s+publish|npm\s+login|npm\s+adduser|npm\s+token\s+(create|revoke)|npm\s+whoami)") | append [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name=".npmrc" AND Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process,"(?i)(npm\s+publish|npm\s+login|npm\s+adduser|npm\s+token\s+(create|revoke)|npm\s+whoami)") | append [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name=".npmrc" AND Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`]
npm install with --ignore-scripts=false or NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS override AIWeaponization High
Catches explicit attempts to re-enable lifecycle scripts that npm 12 disables by default - via --ignore-scripts=false CLI flag, NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS=false env var, or the new approve-scripts opt-in path. After the v12 upgrade rolls out, an adversary with code-exec on a developer box needs to flip this back on to land lifecycle-based persistence. Rationale: Article explicitly names --ignore-scripts as the flag npm 12's new default replaces, and references npm approve-scripts --allow-scripts-pending as the opt-in. NPM_CONFIG_* envvar form is documented npm config behavior. After the v12 ramp, any of these strings on a developer endpoint is an adversary opting out of the new default. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/github-to-disable-npm-install-scripts.html • https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v10/using-npm/config
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers running npm approve-scripts --allow-scripts-pending as instructed by the GitHub blog during upgrade prep
  • Build scripts that legitimately set NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS=false for native-module builds
  • Dockerfile RUN lines that force --foreground-scripts for log visibility
  • Internal tooling that wraps npm and passes the flag through transparently
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "allow-scripts-pending" and InitiatingProcessParentFileName endswith "\\explorer.exe" and AccountName has_any ("dev","engineer","build"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the user, package set, and whether this was the documented upgrade-prep approve-scripts flow vs a fresh install with the flag flipped. Pull surrounding child processes within +/- 60s. 2) Contain: if not approved, isolate the host and capture node_modules for the project; revoke any tokens present in .npmrc. 3) Hunt: search the fleet for the same flag pattern in the last 30 days, look for the same flag combined with --registry pointing off-mainstream, and check whether the same user/host hit UC1 (lifecycle-script suspicious child) in the same window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--ignore-scripts=false","--ignore-scripts false","ignore-scripts=false","NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS=false","--foreground-scripts","allow-scripts-pending")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe","\\npm.cmd") or ParentProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("--ignore-scripts=false","--ignore-scripts false","ignore-scripts=false","NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS=false","--foreground-scripts","allow-scripts-pending")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd") OR Processes.parent_process_name IN ("npm.exe","node.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process,"(?i)(--ignore-scripts(=|\s+)false|ignore-scripts\s*=\s*false|NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS\s*=\s*false|--foreground-scripts|allow-scripts-pending)")
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

CISA KEV: CVE-2026-10520 — Ivanti Sentry OS Command Injection Vulnerability

CISA KEV
2026-06-11 1 use case 1 technique 2 kill-chain phases detected

Ivanti Sentry (formerly known as MobileIron Sentry) contains an OS command injection vulnerability which could allow a remote unauthenticated user to achieve root-level remote code execution. This vulnerability can be successfully exploited in cases where the Sentry appliance is in an unmanaged state with its endpoints externally reachable. The use of mTLS with EPMM or restricted HTTPS access through Neurons for MDM makes interfaces inaccessible to external actors. Vendor: Ivanti, Product: Sentry. Federal patch due: 2026-06-14.

Vulnerable Baileys npm package present on disk (CVE-2026-48063) AIWeaponization Medium
Hunts hosts where node_modules\baileys or node_modules\@whiskeysockets\baileys is present, surfacing the org's exposure to the protocolMessage / placeholderResendMessage spoofing flaw. Pivot to the package.json on hit to confirm the installed version is < 6.7.22 or in 7.0.0-rc.1..rc11. Rationale: References the exact npm package names (baileys, @whiskeysockets/baileys) and the canonical node_modules install path from the GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg advisory. Vulnerability advisories without active campaign IOCs are best served by exposure-mapping hunts — this gives the SOC a host list to drive the patching workstream. Cross-checked against the Baileys releases page where 7.0.0-rc12 / 6.7.22 are noted as the fixed versions. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg • https://github.com/WhiskeySockets/Baileys/releases • https://github.com/WhiskeySockets/Baileys/commit/3beb08eecfcb4e65722e674034bd84fb11a9de35
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Already-patched hosts where package.json reflects baileys >= 6.7.22 or >= 7.0.0-rc12 (analyst must read the version field to filter)
  • Developer laptops with cached test installs that are never run as long-lived sessions
  • CI/CD build agents that fetch and discard dependencies per-build
  • Docker layer scans on a host running container scanning that touch ephemeral node_modules dirs
  • Backup/restore jobs surfacing historical package.json copies
Suppression filter
// Suppress build agents and ephemeral container layers
| where DeviceName !has "build-agent"
| where FolderPath !has @"\.cache\"
| where FolderPath !has "/.npm/_cacache/"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("dockerd.exe", "containerd.exe", "docker", "containerd")
Response runbook
1) Triage: SSH/console onto the host and `cat` the matched package.json — confirm the `version` field is in the vulnerable range (< 6.7.22 OR 7.0.0-rc.1..rc11). For most matches, this is a patch-mgmt task, not an incident. 2) Contain: if the host is an internet-facing Baileys bot/integration on a vulnerable version, coordinate with the owning team to roll to 7.0.0-rc12 / 6.7.22, or apply the interim workaround (drop messages.upsert events with a `requestId` field; set `shouldSyncHistoryMessage: () => false`). 3) Hunt: pivot to UC3 to check whether any spoofed messages.upsert events have already been delivered to this host; pivot to UC2 to find recent installs that introduced the vulnerable version.
// CVE-2026-48063 — Baileys vulnerable package on-disk inventory
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| where FileName =~ "package.json"
| where FolderPath has @"\node_modules\baileys\"
    or FolderPath has @"\node_modules\@whiskeysockets\baileys\"
    or FolderPath has "/node_modules/baileys/"
    or FolderPath has "/node_modules/@whiskeysockets/baileys/"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            Installers = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 10),
            InstallCmds = make_set(InitiatingProcessCommandLine, 5)
            by DeviceName, FolderPath
| order by FirstSeen asc
// CVE-2026-48063 — Baileys vulnerable package on-disk inventory (ASIM)
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified")
| where TargetFileName =~ "package.json"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\node_modules\baileys\"
    or TargetFilePath has @"\node_modules\@whiskeysockets\baileys\"
    or TargetFilePath has "/node_modules/baileys/"
    or TargetFilePath has "/node_modules/@whiskeysockets/baileys/"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            Installers = make_set(ActingProcessName, 10)
            by DvcHostname, TargetFilePath
| order by FirstSeen asc

npm/yarn/pnpm install or upgrade of Baileys package AIInstallation Medium
Detects in-flight installation or upgrade of the Baileys npm package via npm/yarn/pnpm so the SOC can flag new vulnerable deployments and verify the chosen version is the patched 6.7.22 / 7.0.0-rc12+. Complements the on-disk inventory hunt by catching introductions in real time. Rationale: Targets the exact package name strings (baileys, @whiskeysockets/baileys) from the advisory and the standard npm / yarn / pnpm install verbs. Catches new vulnerable deployments before they're hit, supplementing the on-disk inventory pivot. Cross-checked against the GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg affected-packages block. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg • https://www.npmjs.com/package/@whiskeysockets/baileys
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate teams installing the patched 6.7.22 or 7.0.0-rc12+ version (analyst must check the version specifier in cmdline)
  • CI/CD pipeline runs that `npm install` baileys on every build
  • Developer workstations running `npm update` broadly across all deps
  • Dependabot/Renovate auto-PR scripts running `npm install` to validate
  • First-time install commands on a freshly bootstrapped repo
Suppression filter
// Exclude installs that explicitly pin a patched version
| where ProcessCommandLine !contains "baileys@6.7.22"
| where ProcessCommandLine !contains "baileys@7.0.0-rc12"
| where ProcessCommandLine !contains "baileys@latest"
// Exclude known build agents
| where DeviceName !has "ci-runner"
| where DeviceName !has "build-agent"
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the captured cmdline — if it pins a patched version (`baileys@6.7.22`, `baileys@^7.0.0-rc12`, `baileys@latest` post-2026-06-10), close as benign. 2) Contain: if a vulnerable pin is being introduced, contact the developer/owner and have them re-pin to 6.7.22 / 7.0.0-rc12 before merging. 3) Hunt: cross-reference DeviceName against UC1 inventory to confirm the on-disk version after the install completes; pivot to UC3 if this host runs a long-lived Baileys session.
// CVE-2026-48063 — Baileys npm install / upgrade hunt
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","node.exe","npm","yarn","pnpm","node")
    or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","node.exe","npm","yarn","pnpm","node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "baileys"
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "baileys"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("install"," add "," i ","update","upgrade")
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install"," add "," i ","update","upgrade")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
// CVE-2026-48063 — Baileys npm install / upgrade hunt (ASIM)
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)(npm|yarn|pnpm|node)(\.exe)?$"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "baileys"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install"," add "," i ","update","upgrade")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","node.exe","npm","yarn","pnpm","node","npm-cli.js")) AND (Processes.process="*baileys*" OR Processes.process="*@whiskeysockets/baileys*") AND (Processes.process="*install*" OR Processes.process="* add *" OR Processes.process="* i *" OR Processes.process="*update*" OR Processes.process="*upgrade*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

Baileys messages.upsert event carrying a requestId field (exploit signature) AIActions on Objectives High
Direct exploit signature for CVE-2026-48063: the advisory's own workaround is to drop `messages.upsert` events that contain a `requestId` field — meaning that combination is the placeholderResendMessage abuse fingerprint. Hunts forwarded Node.js / Baileys application logs for that pairing on any host running the library. Rationale: Sourced directly from the advisory's workaround text: "dropping messages.upsert events that contain a requestId field" — i.e. Baileys' own maintainers identify the requestId-on-upsert pairing as the exploit signature. No detection guesswork; this is the article's named indicator. Defender Advanced Hunting has no general app-log table so defender_kql is left empty (call it out for SOC consumers running on Defender-only telemetry); Sigma is skipped because the detection needs a custom app-log logsource without a settled category. Falcon LogScale similarly only sees this if the consumer ships Node.js stdout to NG-SIEM ingest. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg • https://github.com/WhiskeySockets/Baileys/commit/3beb08eecfcb4e65722e674034bd84fb11a9de35
ATT&CKT1565.001 T1566 T1059.007
Data sourcesWeb Application
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Baileys debug logging enabled where `requestId` appears in unrelated socket protocol messages logged alongside (not actually on the upsert event) — verify the JSON nesting
  • Internal QA / red-team replay of historical exploit PoCs against staging Baileys instances
  • Patched Baileys (>= 6.7.22 / >= 7.0.0-rc12) re-logging dropped events for audit visibility — workaround behavior, not exploitation
  • Verbose log dumps where a single SyslogMessage line includes multiple unrelated event types and both strings coincidentally appear
Suppression filter
// Suppress patched-version hosts that may still log dropped events for visibility
| where Detail !has "dropped due to requestId"
| where Detail !has "workaround:placeholderResend"
// Suppress QA replay rigs
| where Computer !has "qa-baileys"
| where Computer !has "redteam-"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the matching log line and confirm the `requestId` field is structurally inside the `messages.upsert` event object (not a separate adjacent log entry). Capture the spoofed message key, sender JID, and any payload. 2) Contain: if the host is on a vulnerable Baileys version (cross-ref UC1), upgrade immediately to 6.7.22 / 7.0.0-rc12 OR deploy the workaround (`shouldSyncHistoryMessage: () => false` + drop messages.upsert with requestId in the consumer). Treat any business decisions made on the basis of received WhatsApp messages on this host as untrusted from the time of first hit. 3) Hunt: pivot to all peer JIDs that received the spoofed upsert; check app-state-sync logs for cascading key-share or history-sync events around the same timestamp, since the same exploit also corrupts app state sync.
// CVE-2026-48063 — messages.upsert event with requestId field == placeholderResendMessage exploit signature
// Requires Baileys consumer apps to forward stdout/debug logs to Sentinel via Syslog or CEF
let baileys_exploit =
    Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where SyslogMessage has "messages.upsert"
    | where SyslogMessage has "requestId"
    | extend Source = "Syslog"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, Source, ProcessName, Detail = SyslogMessage;
let baileys_exploit_cef =
    CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where Message has "messages.upsert"
    | where Message has "requestId"
    | extend Source = "CommonSecurityLog"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer = DeviceExternalID, HostIP = SourceIP, Source, ProcessName, Detail = Message;
union baileys_exploit, baileys_exploit_cef
| order by TimeGenerated desc
(source:nodejs OR source:linux.syslog OR source:docker OR source:pm2) "messages.upsert" "requestId"
APPLICATION

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).

Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

JDY botnet distributed reconnaissance scan against perimeter from SOHO IP cohort AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects the JDY hallmark scan shape: many distinct external residential/SOHO source IPs probing the same destination port across the perimeter in a short window. JDY distributes scanning across 1,500+ compromised US/BR SOHO devices specifically to evade IP-reputation and geofence controls, so the cohort-of-sources signal is more reliable than any single IP. Rationale: Cohort detection keys directly on the article's central claim: 1,500+ SOHO bots distributed across US/BR specifically to defeat single-IP reputation controls. Threshold tuned around JDY's described targeted-fingerprinting cadence — high enough to skip individual researcher scans but low enough that a coordinated cohort touching <2% of the botnet still trips it.
ATT&CKT1595.001 T1595.002 T1590
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Shodan / Censys / Project Sonar internet-wide scans (often dozens of source IPs)
  • Cloudflare/Akamai/Fastly edge probes against public-facing assets
  • Authorized red-team or third-party attack-surface vendor scans
  • Botnet IP-churn that legitimately also includes researcher IPs
  • Misconfigured internal load-balancer that NATs many client IPs into a single egress hit on the perimeter
Suppression filter
| where not (SourceIP in ("198.20.69.0/24","198.20.70.0/24","71.6.146.0/24","71.6.158.0/24","66.240.192.0/22")) // Shodan/Censys/Sonar known scanner CIDRs
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the source-IP set and enrich via WHOIS / passive DNS — confirm the cohort lands on residential ISPs in US/BR (Comcast, Spectrum, Vivo, Claro) rather than known scanner ASNs. Check whether the targeted port matches a freshly disclosed edge-device CVE (start with CVE-2026-35616). 2) Contain: if cohort confirmed, geoblock the source ASNs at the WAF/firewall, drop ingress to the targeted port from external networks where business allows, and confirm none of the cohort IPs successfully completed a TCP session beyond SYN+ACK on the targeted asset. 3) Hunt: pivot on each cohort source IP across the last 30 days for any successful auth, any outbound connection from the asset back to the same /24, and any DNS query for the asset's hostname — JDY uses scan results to feed downstream exploitation pipelines, so a successful match upgrades this from recon to imminent intrusion.

Internet-facing edge devices exposing CVE-2026-35616 (JDY weaponization target) AIWeaponization High
Hunts for the specific edge-device CVE JDY operators are actively weaponising to recruit new bots. The article calls out CVE-2026-35616 as the entry vector that triggers shell-script dropper delivery against unpatched SOHO/IoT devices — so any internet-facing inventory match is a pre-compromise alert worth a same-day patch cycle. Rationale: CVE-2026-35616 is the only specific exploit IOC in the article. Pivot scopes to internet-facing assets and to the exact vendor list the article names (Cisco RV320/RV325, Araknis, Mimosa, Ubiquiti, DrayTek, Hikvision, Linksys), which is what JDY targets. Hunting tier because the alert fires on inventory state, not behaviour.
ATT&CKT1190 T1592.002
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Asset inventory stale — device already patched but the CMDB hasn't updated yet
  • Internal-only device misclassified as internet-facing by the IsInternetFacing heuristic
  • End-of-life device with no available patch (true positive but ungovernable — needs compensating control)
  • Vendor mis-attribution where a third-party rebrands one of the listed vendors' silicon
  • DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities lag for newly-published CVEs (false negatives more than positives)
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceCategory == "Endpoint" and IsInternetFacing == false) // suppress patched/non-edge assets misreported by stale TVM data
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify the vulnerable device is reachable from the public internet (curl from an out-of-band host) and confirm the vendor advisory matches CVE-2026-35616. Pull the device's WAN-side ACL to see what ports are exposed. 2) Contain: apply the vendor patch immediately; if patching is blocked, restrict WAN-side management interfaces (HTTP/HTTPS/SSH/Telnet) to a management VLAN or jump host, and consider taking the device offline if it has no business reason to be internet-facing. 3) Hunt: check the device for indicators of prior compromise — review its outbound connections for the last 7 days for connections to Tor entry nodes (the article calls out Tor-based C2 and payload servers), look for unexpected scan-like outbound TCP SYN bursts (see UC3), and inspect for unsigned MIPS-architecture binaries in writable directories.

Internal SOHO/IoT host scanning external destinations (JDY botnet member behaviour) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects an internal asset performing the high-fanout TCP scanning pattern the article attributes to JDY-conscripted bots — many distinct external destinations on a small set of common service ports, sustained over 15–30 minutes. Flags corporate routers, cameras, printers, NVRs and other SOHO/IoT assets that may have been recruited into the botnet's scanner fleet. Rationale: The article describes high-volume TCP/SSL/UDP/ICMP probing across many targets — a small port-set with huge destination fanout is the structural fingerprint. Scoping the source to non-endpoint asset categories (IoT/printer/camera/router) is what makes this distinct from generic outbound scan detection and lines it up with the SOHO/IoT bot population JDY recruits.
ATT&CKT1071 T1046 T1095
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Asset-management or vulnerability scanner running from a misclassified subnet
  • NTP / DNS / NDI broadcast traffic from multicast-heavy IoT devices misread as scanning
  • P2P video conferencing endpoint (Polycom, Crestron) reaching many STUN/TURN destinations
  • Smart TV / streaming device making many CDN connections
  • Backup appliance replicating to a large object-storage destination set
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ((_GetWatchlist('vuln_scanners') | project SearchKey)) // suppress known authorised scanner sources
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the device by MAC/DHCP lease and the vendor OUI. If it's a SOHO router, IP camera, NVR or any of the article's named vendor families (Cisco RV320/RV325, Araknis, Mimosa, Ubiquiti, DrayTek, Hikvision, Linksys), escalate immediately. Pull a 24h packet sample of its egress to confirm the destinations are unrelated to its business purpose. 2) Contain: quarantine the device on a switch ACL or NAC policy, block its egress at the firewall, and physically locate it for offline forensics. Do NOT factory-reset before imaging — the article notes the malware self-deletes after launch, so persistence may live only in non-volatile config. 3) Hunt: search for the same fanout shape across the entire IoT VLAN (same vendor families often share firmware-level exposures), check whether the device's WAN-side admin port is reachable from the internet, and review whether it appears in UC2's CVE-2026-35616 exposure list.
let ScanWindow = 30m;
imNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where NetworkProtocol =~ "TCP"
| where ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr) == true
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize DistinctDsts = dcount(DstIpAddr),
            DistinctPorts = dcount(DstPortNumber),
            SamplePorts = make_set(DstPortNumber, 10),
            SampleDsts = make_set(DstIpAddr, 10),
            ConnCount = count()
            by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, bin(TimeGenerated, ScanWindow)
| where DistinctDsts >= 200 and DistinctPorts <= 5 and ConnCount >= 500
| order by DistinctDsts desc

MIPS/MIPSel architecture-specific payload write (JDY shell-script dropper indicator) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for file writes of MIPS/MIPSel architecture binaries — uncommon outside of router/IoT firmware development. The JDY shell-script dropper specifically downloads architecture-matched payloads (mips, mips64, mipsel, mipsel64) and the article notes the binary is deleted from disk immediately after launch, so any file-event capture is high-signal. Rationale: MIPS/MIPSel naming is the article's explicit architecture token list for the JDY dropper's payload selection. On a standard corporate fleet (x86_64 Windows/Linux/macOS) these strings should not appear in file writes — the false-positive surface is essentially embedded-Linux build environments and firmware repositories, which the filter excludes. Pairs with FileOriginUrl to attribute the download source.
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.004 T1027.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Embedded-Linux developer building OpenWRT / BuildRoot / Yocto images that produce MIPS toolchain output
  • Vendor firmware update download for a managed Cisco/Ubiquiti/DrayTek device
  • Security researcher / sandbox analyst staging malware samples in a lab environment
  • Backup of a router config archive labelled with its architecture
  • Git clone of a public IoT-malware repo for research purposes
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/openwrt/","/buildroot/","/yocto/","/srv/build/") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("make ARCH=mips","crosstool-ng","openwrt-sdk")) // exclude legitimate embedded-Linux toolchain output
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writing process and the device role — a developer laptop running an OpenWRT build is benign; a Linux container or a quarantined IoT asset writing MIPS files to /tmp is not. Cross-reference FileOriginUrl/FileOriginIP against threat intel and check whether the source IP appears in any UC1 cohort. 2) Contain: if non-developer asset, isolate immediately, preserve the file (the article notes self-deletion, so racing to copy it matters) and capture memory if the process is still resident. Block the download URL at the proxy. 3) Hunt: pivot on the FileOriginIP across the last 30 days for any other internal asset that downloaded from the same source, look for child processes of the dropper that match wget/curl + chmod + execute patterns typical of shell-script droppers, and feed the FileOriginIP back into UC3 to check whether the host began scanning shortly after.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName matches regex @"(?i)(^|[\._\-])(mips|mipsel|mips64|mipsel64)([\._\-]|$)"
   or FileOriginUrl matches regex @"(?i)(^|[\._\-/])(mips|mipsel|mips64|mipsel64)([\._\-/?]|$)"
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/usr/lib/firmware","/var/lib/firmware","/opt/openwrt","buildroot"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
imFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType =~ "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)(^|[\._\-])(mips|mipsel|mips64|mipsel64)([\._\-]|$)"
| where not (ActingProcessName has_any ("openwrt","buildroot","yocto"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSize, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: MIPS Architecture Binary Written to Disk Indicating IoT/SOHO Botnet Dropper
id: c1f4e3a2-8b6d-4e1f-9c2a-7d3b8e5a1c4f
description: Detects creation of files whose name carries a MIPS/MIPSel architecture token (mips, mipsel, mips64, mipsel64). The JDY botnet's shell-script dropper downloads architecture-matched payloads to recruit edge devices and self-deletes the binary after launch, so file-create capture is high-signal.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/china-linked-jdy-botnet-expands-to-1500.html
author: Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/17
tags:
  - attack.command_and_control
  - attack.t1105
  - attack.t1059.004
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: linux
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|re|i: '(^|.*[\._\-/])(mips|mipsel|mips64|mipsel64)([\._\-/]|$)'
  filter_buildtools:
    Image|contains:
      - '/openwrt/'
      - '/buildroot/'
      - '/yocto/'
  condition: selection and not filter_buildtools
level: medium

source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:PATH (@file.path:*mips* OR @file.path:*mipsel* OR @file.path:*mips64* OR @file.path:*mipsel64*) -@process.executable.path:/openwrt/* -@process.executable.path:/buildroot/*
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| regex("(?i)(^|[\\._\\-/])(mips|mipsel|mips64|mipsel64)([\\._\\-/]|$)", field=TargetFileName)
| NOT (ContextImageFileName=/openwrt/i OR ContextImageFileName=/buildroot/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(Filesystem.file_path) AS paths, values(Filesystem.process_name) AS writers from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action="created" (Filesystem.file_name="*.mips" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.mipsel" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.mips64" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.mipsel64" OR Filesystem.file_name="*mips_*" OR Filesystem.file_name="*mipsel_*" OR Filesystem.file_name="*-mips-*" OR Filesystem.file_name="*-mipsel-*") by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.file_name, _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | join type=left dest [ search index=web earliest=-1h (uri_path="*mips*" OR uri_path="*mipsel*") | stats values(url) AS download_url values(src) AS download_src by dest ] | table _time, dest, user, file_name, paths, writers, download_url

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)

| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
