   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

Ivanti, Fortinet, and SAP Release Patches for Multiple Critical Vulnerabilities

The Hacker News
2026-06-10 8 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Fortinet, Ivanti, and SAP have released security updates to address multiple critical security vulnerabilities that could result in arbitrary code execution and information disclosure. The security flaw patched by Fortinet relates to a command injection vulnerability in FortiSandbox, FortiSandbox Cloud, and FortiSandbox PaaS WEB UI. It's tracked as CVE-2026-25089 (CVSS score: 9.1). Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Pre-patch Ivanti Sentry / FortiSandbox / SAP NetWeaver versions exposed to the article CVEs · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Ivanti Sentry CVE-2026-10520 exploit attempt via /mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Ivanti Sentry CVE-2026-10520 exploit attempt via /mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage AIExploitation High
Detects HTTP requests to the Ivanti Sentry (formerly MobileIron Sentry) unauthenticated MICS configuration endpoint that is parsed by the backend handleExecute() function and yields root-level RCE. The endpoint is documented by watchTowr Labs and confirmed in CISA KEV (added 2026-06-11) — any external hit pre-patch is a near-certain exploitation attempt and any hit post-patch on R10.5.2/R10.6.2/R10.7.1+ should redirect to login per Ivanti's hardening. Rationale: Pivots on the exact endpoint string disclosed in the article and corroborated by watchTowr Labs (which published the PoC on 2026-06-10) and Rapid7. This path is internal-only by design — Ivanti's patch redirects unauthenticated hits to the login page — so any pre-patch hit on production traffic is a high-confidence exploitation attempt; CISA KEV listing on 2026-06-11 confirms active in-the-wild use. Cross-checked against: • https://labs.watchtowr.com/more-evidence-that-words-dont-mean-what-we-thought-they-meant-ivanti-sentry-pre-auth-os-command-injection-cve-2026-10520/ • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-10520-cve-2026-10523-multiple-critical-vulnerabilities-affecting-ivanti-sentry/ • https://www.esentire.com/security-advisories/critical-vulnerabilities-in-ivanti-sentry-cve-2026-10520-cve-2026-10523 • https://github.com/watchtowrlabs/watchTowr-vs-Ivanti-Sentry-RCE-CVE-2026-10520-CVE-2026-10523
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vulnerability scanner (Nessus / Qualys / Rapid7 InsightVM) probing the endpoint as part of authenticated scans
  • Red-team / pentester validating the patch on staging Sentry instances
  • watchTowr's Detection Artefact Generator or proof-of-concept harness run by the IR team for tabletop
  • Authorised CISA / ACSC / NCSC scanning of internet-facing inventory (e.g. Censys-style attack-surface bots)
  • Patch verification tools (Tenable, Rapid7) calling the endpoint to confirm post-patch redirect to login
Suppression filter
// Append to the union sentinel_kql to suppress known-good scanners and admin hosts:
// | where SrcIpAddr !in ("10.10.0.5","10.10.0.6")        // sentry-admin jump boxes
// | where UA !has "Nessus" and UA !has "Qualys" and UA !has "InsightVM"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full request (method, body, status code) and source IP. Compare source IP to allow-listed admin jump boxes and approved scanners. HTTP 200 on a pre-patch (<R10.5.2 / <R10.6.2 / <R10.7.1) Sentry strongly implies successful RCE; 302→login on a patched build is harmless. Capture the `message` parameter value if logged — it carries the OS command payload. 2) CONTAIN: If source is unknown/external, block the IP at the perimeter and isolate the Sentry appliance from the internet until version is confirmed patched. If pre-patch, treat the appliance as compromised, snapshot for IR, then rebuild from gold image. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the appliance for: new local/admin accounts created via CVE-2026-10523 auth bypass (paired vuln), unexpected outbound connections from the Sentry host, novel processes / cron entries, and modifications to MICS config files. Check downstream managed-device traffic for unauthorised MDM policy pushes.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage"
   or AdditionalFields has "mics-config/handleMessage"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessAccountSid
| order by Timestamp desc
// Primary: ASIM web session (covers WAF/proxy/IIS via parsers). Falls back to CommonSecurityLog and W3CIISLog.
let vuln_path = "/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage";
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImWebSession
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where Url has vuln_path
   | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url,
             HttpStatusCode, UA=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, EventVendor, EventProduct,
             SourceTable="ImWebSession"),
  (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where RequestURL has vuln_path or Message has vuln_path
   | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr=SourceIP, DstIpAddr=DestinationIP,
             DstHostname=DestinationHostName, HttpMethod=RequestMethod, Url=RequestURL,
             HttpStatusCode=tostring(EventOutcome), UA=RequestClientApplication,
             EventVendor=DeviceVendor, EventProduct=DeviceProduct,
             SourceTable="CommonSecurityLog"),
  (W3CIISLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where csUriStem has vuln_path
   | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr=cIP, DstIpAddr="", DstHostname=Computer,
             HttpMethod=csMethod, Url=strcat(csUriStem, iff(isnotempty(csUriQuery), strcat("?", csUriQuery), "")),
             HttpStatusCode=tostring(scStatus), UA=csUserAgent,
             EventVendor="Microsoft", EventProduct="IIS", SourceTable="W3CIISLog")
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Ivanti Sentry CVE-2026-10520 Pre-Auth RCE Exploit Attempt
id: 9d1f2c4a-6a8e-4b3c-9f2d-22b5c8e9f001
description: Detects HTTP requests to the Ivanti Sentry unauthenticated MICS configuration endpoint /mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage which is parsed by the backend handleExecute() function and yields root-level command injection per watchTowr Labs research and CISA KEV.

Pre-patch Ivanti Sentry / FortiSandbox / SAP NetWeaver versions exposed to the article CVEs AIReconnaissance High
Inventory hunt that flags devices still running the affected versions called out in the article for CVE-2026-25089 (FortiSandbox), CVE-2026-10520 & CVE-2026-10523 (Ivanti Sentry), CVE-2026-44748 / -27671 / -22732 / -40128 (SAP NetWeaver & Commerce Cloud). Drives both prioritised patching and feeds UC1 with a list of likely targets — assets that show up here AND get hit by the endpoint detection are de-facto incidents. Rationale: Article enumerates the exact affected product versions (FortiSandbox 5.0.0–5.0.5 / 4.4.0–4.4.8, Sentry pre-R10.5.2/R10.6.2/R10.7.1, SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP / Java / Commerce Cloud) and seven CVE identifiers. TVM-style hunting against this exact CVE set tells the SOC which assets are at risk and feeds UC1 — devices on this list that also surface in the Ivanti endpoint UC are confirmed exploitation candidates. Cross-checked against Rapid7 and eSentire advisories for the Ivanti versions and Onapsis briefing for the SAP set. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-10520-cve-2026-10523-multiple-critical-vulnerabilities-affecting-ivanti-sentry/ • https://www.esentire.com/security-advisories/critical-vulnerabilities-in-ivanti-sentry-cve-2026-10520-cve-2026-10523
ATT&CKT1190 T1592.002
Data sourcesVulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Lab / dev / staging appliances intentionally held back from the patch cycle for regression testing
  • SAP NetWeaver instances pending a scheduled change window (SAP patching cadence is typically monthly post-Patch-Tuesday)
  • Air-gapped / segmented FortiSandbox instances whose risk profile already accepts delayed patching
  • Vendor support engagements where the OEM has requested the version be retained for diagnostics
  • Devices flagged by TVM but already protected by compensating WAF rules / pre-auth controls
Suppression filter
// Strip lab/staging from the result set:
// | where DeviceName !startswith "lab-" and DeviceName !startswith "stg-" and DeviceName !startswith "test-"
// | where MachineGroup !in ("Lab","Staging","PreProd")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Sort the result set by IsInternetFacing == true, then by CVSS. Confirm RecommendedSecurityUpdate has shipped to the patch-management system (Ivanti EPM / Intune / SAP Solution Manager). Identify business owner per asset. 2) CONTAIN: For internet-facing pre-patch Ivanti Sentry → block 443/inbound at edge until patched (CISA KEV 3-day mandate applies to federal; treat as hard SLA). FortiSandbox WEB UI → restrict to admin VLAN only. SAP NetWeaver → restrict RFC gateway and Java web container to known clients via secinfo/reginfo until patched. 3) HUNT: For every asset on this list, run UC1's Ivanti endpoint query over the last 60 days. For SAP rows, search OfficeActivity / SAP audit logs for anomalous SAML logins (CVE-2026-44748 signature wrapping) or unexpected RFC calls (CVE-2026-27671 memory corruption) from non-corporate source IPs.

title: Entra ID Consent to Third-Party OAuth Application
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05

APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",

    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.

DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"

Arista EOS CVE-2026-7473 - Unexpected Tunneled Traffic to Configured VTEP / GRE AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for VXLAN (UDP/4789) or GRE traffic reaching an Arista 7020R/7280R/7500R VTEP from sources outside the legitimate overlay fabric. Per Arista's advisory the switch decapsulates any tunnel whose outer destination matches the configured decap IP regardless of inner protocol, so any unexpected source contacting the VTEP is a potential exploitation attempt of CVE-2026-7473. Rationale: Arista's published mitigation explicitly names VXLAN (UDP/4789) and GRE as the abusable encapsulations and 7020R/7280R/R2/7500R/R2 as the impacted platforms. Detection pivots on tunnel-destined traffic from non-RFC1918 sources and on EOS syslog where the agent reports the unexpected decap path. Cross-checked against Arista's advisory phrasing in the article. Cross-checked against: • https://www.arista.com/en/support/advisories-notices
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate eVPN/VXLAN peering from a partner ASN whose source range was never added to the IPAM lookup
  • Network engineer testing GRE tunnel from a jump host on a public-IP allocation
  • Cloud-burst overlay where the remote VTEP genuinely lives on a public address (Azure VWAN, AWS Transit Gateway Connect)
  • Monitoring probe (NetSnmp, BFD reflector) issuing VXLAN-encapsulated keepalives
Suppression filter
and not (SourceIP in (toscalar(externaldata(IP:string) [@"https://internal-ipam/known_partner_vteps.csv"] with(format="csv"))))
Response runbook
Step 1 — triage: confirm the destination IP is actually a configured VTEP / GRE endpoint per Arista's advisory list (7020R/7280R/7500R series only); pull the matching EOS flow record and verify the inner protocol is something the overlay should NOT carry. Step 2 — contain: apply the upstream-ACL mitigation Arista recommends — `permit udp <legit-source-block> any eq 4789` then `deny udp any any eq 4789` on the L3 transit interface, plus equivalent GRE filter. Step 3 — hunt: pivot on the source IP across NetFlow for the last 30 days; look for prior reconnaissance (port scans, ICMP probing) and any internal hosts that received decapsulated traffic post-decap.
let arista_hosts = dynamic(["arista","eos","vtep"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(
  Syslog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where HostName has_any (arista_hosts) or Computer has_any (arista_hosts)
  | where SyslogMessage matches regex @"(?i)(VXLAN|GRE|decap|tunnel)"
  | where SyslogMessage matches regex @"(?i)(unexpected|invalid|mismatch|drop|denied|non-configured)"
  | project TimeGenerated, Host=HostName, EvSource="syslog", DestinationPort=int(null), SourceAddr="", DestAddr="", AppProto="", Detail=SyslogMessage
),
(
  CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where DeviceVendor =~ "Arista" or DeviceProduct has "EOS"
  | where DestinationPort == 4789 or ApplicationProtocol has_any ("vxlan","gre")
  | where not(SourceIP startswith "10.") and not(SourceIP startswith "192.168.") and not(SourceIP matches regex @"^172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[0-1])\.")
  | project TimeGenerated, Host=DeviceExternalID, EvSource="cef", DestinationPort, SourceAddr=SourceIP, DestAddr=DestinationIP, AppProto=ApplicationProtocol, Detail=Message
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog (@host.name:*arista* OR @host.name:*vtep* OR @syslog.appname:*Tunnel* OR @syslog.appname:*Decap*) (@syslog.message:*VXLAN* OR @syslog.message:*GRE* OR @syslog.message:*tunnel*) (@syslog.message:*unexpected* OR @syslog.message:*invalid* OR @syslog.message:*mismatch* OR @syslog.message:*non-configured*)

Chrome V8 CVE-2026-11645 - Suspicious non-browser child of chrome.exe (renderer escape) AIExploitation High
V8 OOB read/write inside the renderer sandbox typically chains to a sandbox escape that spawns a non-browser child process. This UC catches chrome.exe / msedge.exe / brave.exe spawning LOLBins or shells immediately after a drive-by visit, which is the post-exploitation pivot for CVE-2026-11645. Rationale: Article confirms CVE-2026-11645 is a V8 OOB read/write actively exploited via crafted HTML — the canonical exploitation tail is a non-browser child of chrome.exe. Chrome's own utility/renderer processes always carry --type= / --utility-sub-type= flags, which we exclude to keep the FP rate near zero. Article cross-referenced with CVE summary on KEV catalog (added 2026-06-10). Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog • https://chromereleases.googleblog.com/
ATT&CKT1203 T1189
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • MDM/EDR agent invoking certutil via a browser-initiated install flow
  • Developer running `chrome.exe --no-sandbox` and chain-launching cmd from devtools-integration extensions
  • Selenium / Playwright test harness driving chromium with custom subprocess hooks
  • Enterprise PKI enrolment pages that legitimately spawn certutil to install a user cert
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--remote-debugging-port","--no-sandbox","--headless") or InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !in~ ("Google LLC","Microsoft Corporation","Brave Software Inc."))
Response runbook
Step 1 — triage: pull the browser version from `InitiatingProcessVersionInfoProductVersion` and check it against the Chrome stable release that ships the CVE-2026-11645 fix; pull the parent browser's URL history for the 60s before the child spawn. Step 2 — contain: isolate the device via Defender Live Response, revoke the user's primary refresh token in Entra ID, force a Chrome auto-update. Step 3 — hunt: 30-day sweep on DeviceNetworkEvents for the device contacting any IP the child process reached out to, plus a tenant-wide search for the same parent-child shape over the last 24h to catch other victims of the same exploit kit.

CISA KEV June 2026 - Vulnerable Cisco SD-WAN / Chrome / Arista assets in inventory AIReconnaissance High
Surfaces every device in the estate still exposed to CVE-2026-20245 (Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager), CVE-2026-11645 (Chrome V8) or CVE-2026-7473 (Arista EOS) — the three CVEs CISA added to KEV on 2026-06-10 with an FCEB remediation deadline of 2026-06-23. Drives patch prioritisation rather than chasing post-compromise tells. Rationale: Article lists the three KEV-added CVEs with their CVSS scores and the FCEB June-23 deadline verbatim. A KEV-exposure hunting rule is the highest-leverage detection a SOC can ship against an article whose primary message is 'patch by date X'. No external corroboration needed beyond the KEV catalog itself. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Decommissioned hosts still reporting via Defender that have since been retired
  • Lab/testbed Arista 7280R intentionally kept on an old EOS build
  • Pre-prod Chrome builds (Beta/Canary) where the vulnerable version is expected
  • SD-WAN appliance flagged but isolated on a management VLAN with no inbound exposure
Response runbook
Step 1 — triage: rank exposed hosts by internet-facing role (DMZ Arista VTEPs > SD-WAN Manager > end-user Chrome installs); cross-reference with DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing where available. Step 2 — contain: for Arista, apply the upstream-ACL mitigation Arista published (no patch is planned); for Chrome, push the auto-update channel; for Cisco SD-WAN Manager, apply Cisco PSIRT's patch. Step 3 — hunt: parallel-launch the Chrome-child and Arista-tunnel UCs above against the exposed-asset list; check Defender alert history (last 14d) for any AlertEvidence already touching these hosts.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Web-facing exposure of dev.env / .env config file (returns 200) AIReconnaissance High
Hunts HTTP requests to dev.env / .env / .env.* paths that returned a 2xx response, indicating a misconfigured web server is leaking the very file that ships AUTH_JWT_SECRET=random. CVE-2026-48031 weaponises exactly this file, so any successful retrieval is a direct precursor to JWT forgery. Rationale: Targets the exact filename (dev.env) named at line 10 of the advisory plus common .env variants the same template is renamed to. 2xx/3xx status confirms the leak actually happened. Cross-checked CVE-2026-48031 advisory and dhax/go-base PR #31. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mqq6-462x-jxmm • https://github.com/dhax/go-base/pull/31
ATT&CKT1592.002 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal CI/CD pipeline pulling .env from a private artifact server
  • DAST/SAST scanners (Burp, ZAP, Nessus) probing for exposed dotfiles
  • Penetration testers running ffuf / dirsearch with default wordlists
  • Internal developer documentation site serving a sanitized .env.example
  • Cloud config-management agents (Consul, etcd) syncing env templates over HTTP
Suppression filter
and csUserAgent !has_any ("Burp","OWASP ZAP","Nessus","Qualys","Nuclei","ffuf","dirsearch","gobuster") and cIP !in (KnownScannerIPs)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pivot on cIP/sourceIPAddress; was the request from a known scanner, a developer subnet, or external? Inspect User-Agent and response size — non-empty 200 on dev.env is critical. 2) Contain: rotate AUTH_JWT_SECRET immediately to a 32+ byte random value, invalidate all outstanding JWT/refresh tokens, and add a WebACL/NGINX deny for .env/dev.env paths. Take the affected service off the perimeter if the secret was leaked externally. 3) Hunt: look for forged-token use — admin API calls from the same source IP within 24h, /api/v1/token/refresh hits with unknown sub claims, and any new sessions whose iat predates the secret rotation. Sweep all Go services for github.com/dhax/go-base in go.mod.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("/dev.env","/.env","/.env.dev","/.env.local","/.env.development")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("code.exe","devenv.exe","goland64.exe","idea64.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, LocalIP
| order by Timestamp desc
// IIS-fronted Go service exposure
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem matches regex @"(?i)(^|/)(dev\.env|\.env(\.[a-z]+)?)$"
| where scStatus in (200,206,301,302)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent
| union (
    CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where DeviceProduct in ("WAF","Application Gateway","CloudFront","NGINX","Apache")
    | where RequestURL matches regex @"(?i)(^|/)(dev\.env|\.env(\.[a-z]+)?)(\?|$)"
    | where toint(EventOutcome) between (200 .. 399)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DeviceName, sSiteName=DestinationHostName, cIP=SourceIP, csMethod=RequestMethod, csUriStem=RequestURL, csUriQuery="", scStatus=toint(EventOutcome), csUserAgent=RequestClientApplication
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Web exposure of dev.env / .env config file
id: 7c1a4b3e-2f57-4c61-9c4e-3a1e2f8b5d11
description: Detects HTTP requests retrieving dev.env or .env files that may leak the hardcoded AUTH_JWT_SECRET=random used by github.com/dhax/go-base (CVE-2026-48031).
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mqq6-462x-jxmm
  - https://github.com/dhax/go-base/pull/31
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/12
tags:
  - attack.reconnaissance
  - attack.t1592.002
  - attack.t1083
  - cve.2026.48031
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection_path:
    cs-uri-stem|re|i: '(^|/)(dev\.env|\.env(\.[a-z]+)?)$'
  selection_status:
    sc-status:
      - 200
      - 206
      - 301
      - 302
  condition: selection_path and selection_status
level: high
(source:nginx OR source:apache OR source:iis OR source:cloudfront OR source:caddy) @http.url_details.path:(*/dev.env OR */.env OR */.env.dev OR */.env.local OR */.env.development) @http.status_code:[200 TO 399]
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| ConnectionDirection=1
| (RemotePort=80 OR RemotePort=443 OR RemotePort=3000 OR RemotePort=8080)
| join({#event_simpleName=DnsRequest | DomainName=/.*/ }, field=[aid], include=[DomainName])
| regex("/(dev\.env|\.env)(\.[a-z]+)?($|\?)", field=CommandLine, strict=false)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())
# log group: /aws/cloudtrail/dataevents (S3 object-level events)
fields @timestamp, eventName, sourceIPAddress, userIdentity.arn, requestParameters.bucketName, requestParameters.key, errorCode
| filter eventSource = "s3.amazonaws.com"
      and eventName in ["GetObject", "GetObjectAcl"]
      and (requestParameters.key like /(?i)(^|\/)(dev\.env|\.env(\.[a-z]+)?)$/)
      and not isPresent(errorCode)
| sort @timestamp desc
| limit 200

github.com/dhax/go-base supply-chain footprint in go.mod / build artifacts AIReconnaissance High
Identifies hosts (developer laptops, CI runners, container build agents) where go.mod, go.sum, vendor/modules.txt or Dockerfiles reference github.com/dhax/go-base. The advisory states 'all versions before commit cc82b974...' are vulnerable, so footprinting the dependency is the first step before patching can begin. Rationale: Anchors on the exact module path github.com/dhax/go-base named in the advisory's Affected Component list. go.mod / go.sum / Dockerfile additions and `go build`/`go mod` invocations that reference the module pin the asset surface that needs patching to the cc82b974... commit. Cross-checked CVE-2026-48031 advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mqq6-462x-jxmm • https://github.com/dhax/go-base/commits/master
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1518
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate developer evaluating the boilerplate for a new microservice
  • Security team running SCA scan that already covers this CVE
  • CI job intentionally pinning to the patched commit (>= cc82b9740fa6)
  • Internal fork of go-base that is already patched
  • Vulnerability scanner (Trivy, Grype, Snyk) reading go.sum files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("trivy.exe","grype.exe","snyk.exe","syft.exe") and AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: list every host/build agent that touched go.mod referencing dhax/go-base in the last 30d. For each, pull the pinned version (the @ pseudo-version after the path). Anything before commit cc82b9740fa6 (2026-05-17) is vulnerable. 2) Contain: file Jira/Linear tickets to bump the dependency past cc82b9740fa6, regenerate AUTH_JWT_SECRET (>=32 chars), and force a token revocation on next deploy. Block new builds on the unpatched version via a renovate/dependabot policy. 3) Hunt: identify all running services derived from the vulnerable code — query container registries for images whose go.mod includes the unpatched pin. For any that were ever internet-facing, run the JWT-forgery UC against their access logs back to the deploy date.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("go.mod","go.sum","modules.txt","Dockerfile")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| union (
    DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where ProcessCommandLine has "dhax/go-base"
       or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "dhax/go-base"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, ActionType="ProcessCmdline", FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ProcessCommandLine
)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("go.mod","go.sum","modules.txt","Dockerfile")
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| union (
    ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has "dhax/go-base"
       or ParentProcessCommandLine has "dhax/go-base"
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath=ActingProcessName, TargetFileName=ActingProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Admin / privileged API call without a preceding SUCCESSFUL login (JWT forgery indicator) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Forged tokens signed with the hardcoded 'random' secret never traverse the application's login or refresh flows — they appear as bearer-auth-only requests. This UC pivots web access logs for /api/v1/admin/* and /api/v1/me hits whose source IP has no /api/v1/login/* 2xx in the prior 24h, the behavioural signature of token forgery. Rationale: The advisory's PoC explicitly hits /api/v1/admin/users, /api/v1/me, and /api/v1/token/refresh with a forged Bearer token (no login step). Modelling 'admin hit without a recent successful login from same IP' captures that footprint without requiring the JWT to be parsed. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mqq6-462x-jxmm
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web Authentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Long-lived legitimate session whose original login was >24h ago (refresh token kept it alive)
  • Service-to-service auth using a static API key rather than the login flow
  • Healthcheck / synthetic monitoring hitting /api/v1/me with a pre-baked token
  • CI smoke tests that obtain tokens out of band and never use /login
  • NAT'd corporate egress where many users share one source IP and not all have logged in
Suppression filter
and csUserName !in ("healthcheck","synthetics","datadog","newrelic") and csUserAgent !has_any ("Pingdom","StatusCake","Datadog Synthetics","kube-probe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the JWT from the Authorization header — decode header+payload (no signature check needed) and verify the 'sub' and 'roles' claims match a real user. Compare 'iat' against the user's last legitimate login from your IdP. 2) Contain: if the token is forged, rotate AUTH_JWT_SECRET to a 32+ byte random value, restart the Go service, and force-revoke all sessions. Block the source IP at the WAF. 3) Hunt: pull all requests from the same IP and from the same user-agent over the prior 30 days. Look for /api/v1/admin/users enumeration, mass /api/v1/me lookups across different sub claims (token re-use across identities), and any state-changing POST/PUT/DELETE that may have already exfiltrated data.
let AdminHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(24h)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any ("/api/v1/admin/","/api/v1/me","/api/v1/token/refresh")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl;
let LoginHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(48h)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any ("/api/v1/login/","/api/v1/auth/")
    | summarize LastLogin = max(Timestamp) by RemoteIP;
AdminHits
| join kind=leftouter LoginHits on RemoteIP
| where isnull(LastLogin) or datetime_diff('hour', Timestamp, LastLogin) > 24
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, LastLogin, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
let AdminHits = W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
    | where csUriStem matches regex @"(?i)/api/v1/(admin/|me$|token/refresh)"
    | where scStatus < 400
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, csUriStem, csUserAgent, csUserName;
let LoginHits = W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(48h)
    | where csUriStem matches regex @"(?i)/api/v1/(login|auth)"
    | where scStatus < 400
    | summarize LastLogin = max(TimeGenerated) by cIP;
AdminHits
| join kind=leftouter LoginHits on cIP
| where isnull(LastLogin) or datetime_diff('hour', TimeGenerated, LastLogin) > 24
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, csUriStem, csUserAgent, csUserName, LastLogin

Internal host clones / curls github.com/dhax/go-base or raw dev.env AIReconnaissance Medium
Catches developer or attacker hosts pulling the vulnerable boilerplate — either via 'git clone github.com/dhax/go-base', 'go get', or direct curl/wget of raw.githubusercontent.com/dhax/go-base/.../dev.env. Either action seeds the secret 'random' onto a system that may later run the service or be used to forge tokens. Rationale: Hits the exact module path github.com/dhax/go-base from the advisory's Affected Component plus the raw.githubusercontent.com pattern used when an attacker just wants the leaked dev.env without cloning. Narrowing to git/go/curl/wget keeps the volume sane. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mqq6-462x-jxmm • https://github.com/dhax/go-base

Response runbook
1) Triage: validate the host — is it a dev workstation, a build agent, or a production server? Production server is the worst case. Capture the destination path of the clone to know where the secret 'random' now lives on disk. 2) Contain: if production, rip out the deployed artifact and rebuild from a patched commit (>= cc82b9740fa6). On dev hosts, ensure the dev.env file is not later copied into a release container. 3) Hunt: from the same host/user, look for subsequent 'go build' artifacts being pushed to internal registries, container image pushes labelled with the developer's name, and any web service deployed from those artifacts now serving /api/v1/* on the network.

JWT token in HTTP Authorization header verifying against secret 'random' AIActions on Objectives High
Decodes Bearer JWTs from web access logs and verifies their HMAC-SHA256 signature against the literal key 'random'. A successful verification is a smoking-gun forged token from the public CVE-2026-48031 secret. This is the highest-confidence detection but requires a custom enrichment step in the SIEM ingestion pipeline. Rationale: Implements the article's exact PoC inversely — the attacker uses 'random' as the HMAC key to sign; we use it to verify. Any token that verifies with key='random' is, by definition, a forged token because patched versions log.Fatal on that secret. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mqq6-462x-jxmm • https://github.com/dhax/go-base/pull/31
ATT&CKT1606.001 T1550.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal pentester actively exploiting the CVE during an authorised engagement
  • Pre-prod environment that still ships the unpatched dev.env intentionally for testing
  • Bug-bounty researcher submitting a PoC against the production endpoint
  • An unrelated service that coincidentally also uses HS256 with the (weak) key 'random' for a different purpose
  • Token-replay testing tools (e.g. Burp JWT extension) being run by red team

and SourceIP !in (KnownPenTesterIPs) and not (Environment == "staging" and ServiceName startswith "goose-base-test-")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the affected endpoint is running github.com/dhax/go-base. Decode the JWT 'sub' and 'roles' claims and check whether they correspond to a real user or a fabricated identity. Any 'roles' containing 'admin' is automatic priority-1. 2) Contain: rotate AUTH_JWT_SECRET to `openssl rand -base64 32`, redeploy the service to invalidate all outstanding tokens, force-logout all users, then patch the dhax/go-base dependency past commit cc82b9740fa6. Block the source IP at the WAF. 3) Hunt: pull every request from the offending IP over 30d; cross-correlate with DB audit logs for /api/v1/admin/users access, profile reads (/api/v1/me), and any state-mutating POST/PUT/DELETE. Identify what was touched and prepare a breach-notification scope.

Compromised Rust crate onering performs code exfiltration

Aikido
2026-06-10 8 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The compromised onering Rust crate v1.4.1 on crates.io shipped a malicious build.rs that exfiltrates the diff of your latest commit to a hosted Sentry endpoint every time you build. Category: Vulnerabilities & Threats

ATT&CKT1176 T1190 T1195.002
Domainso4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Cargo dependency manifest or download pinned to compromised onering 1.4.1
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Network egress to onering Sentry exfil ingest domain or project envelope path · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Cargo build script spawning git with onering's exfil --pretty=format JSON · [LLM] build.rs invoking curl POST to Sentry envelope endpoint with code diff payload · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Cargo build script spawning git with onering's exfil --pretty=format JSON AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the onering 1.4.1 build.rs harvesting host repo metadata by spawning `git log -n 1 --pretty=format:{"commit":"%H","author":"%an",...}` from a Cargo build-script process. The JSON pretty-format template plus a Cargo build-script parent is the article-specific fingerprint of the exfil step. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim --pretty=format JSON template strings the article shows in the build.rs payload (`commit`, `%H`, `author`, `%an`, `email`, `%ae`) combined with a Cargo build-script parent (rustc compiles build.rs to a binary named `build-script-build` on Windows/Linux). Routine `git log` calls from IDEs/CI don't carry this exact JSON tag set parented by a build-script process. Cross-checked the build-script-build naming via the official Cargo build-script reference (doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-scripts.html) and the upstream maintainer issue https://github.com/cenotelie/onering/issues/1. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/cenotelie/onering/issues/1 • https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-scripts.html
ATT&CKT1005 T1195.001 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer tooling (rust-analyzer, IDE git extensions) running git log with --pretty=format but using a CSV/tab template, not the JSON tag set above
  • CI scripts running git log --pretty=format from a shell, not parented by build-script-build
  • Custom internal Rust crates whose legitimate build.rs invokes git for version-stamping (usually only `git rev-parse HEAD`, not multi-field JSON metadata)
  • Cargo workspace tooling like `cargo-edit` or `cargo-release` shelling out to git from rustc context
  • Manual test of the cenotelie/onering repository itself by a researcher reproducing the IOC
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "rev-parse" and not (ProcessCommandLine has_all ("%H", "%an", "%ae")))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture full process tree (cargo→rustc→build-script-build→git), the Cargo.lock and Cargo.toml on the host, and the user's home repo path; confirm `onering` 1.4.1 is in the dependency graph (`cargo tree | grep onering`). 2) Contain: isolate the dev workstation from the network, kill the cargo build, revoke any source-control PATs the user has cached (gh, git credential-manager), and force-push-protect any branches the user touched in the last 24h. 3) Hunt: query DeviceNetworkEvents for the same DeviceId reaching o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io or any /api/4511539669368912/envelope/ POST in the last 30 days, pivot on every other host that resolved that domain, and search Cargo.lock files repo-wide for `onering` at v1.4.1.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("git.exe", "git")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "log"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--pretty=format"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_all ("commit", "%H", "author", "%an", "email", "%ae")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("build-script-build.exe", "build_script_build.exe", "build-script-build", "cargo.exe", "rustc.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

build.rs invoking curl POST to Sentry envelope endpoint with code diff payload AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the onering build.rs exfiltration POST: curl invoked with the specific Sentry envelope URL (project id 4511539669368912 / org id o4511539639222272) and the `application/x-sentry-envelope` Content-Type, parented by a Cargo build-script process. This is the network-layer half of the exfil chain. Rationale: Article gives the verbatim Sentry ingest URL, DSN public key, organization id and project id. Curl parented by a Cargo build-script with any of those four strings in the cmdline is essentially deterministic for the onering payload. The combination forecloses noise from legit Sentry users (none would have curl invoked by build-script-build) and from legit Cargo builds (none would POST to a Sentry envelope). Cross-checked the Sentry envelope endpoint format at docs.sentry.io/api/envelopes/. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.sentry.io/api/envelopes/ • https://github.com/cenotelie/onering/issues/1
ATT&CKT1041 T1567 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Project legitimately using Sentry crash-reporting from Rust code, but invoked via the sentry-rust SDK at runtime (not via curl in a build script)
  • Developer manually testing the IOC for IR/research purposes from the same host
  • Internal Sentry-on-prem mirror where the URL happens to contain the same project id substring
  • Penetration-test simulation of supply-chain exfil using these exact IOCs
  • Threat-intel platform crawler fetching the article URL into a curl trace logged by EDR
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the curl process tree, extract the POST body if proxy/PCAP available, and confirm the DSN public key 8197ee42c4f59c83f4cc6d48f5bae821 in the URL path. Pull Cargo.lock on the host and grep for `onering`. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the cargo build, block o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io at the proxy, rotate any source-tree secrets the recent commit may have touched (treat the recent diff as exposed). 3) Hunt: pivot DeviceNetworkEvents on the destination domain across the fleet for the last 30 days; pivot on every internal repo whose Cargo.lock contains onering 1.4.1; alert affected dev leads that recent commits leaked.
DeviceProcessEvents

Network egress to onering Sentry exfil ingest domain or project envelope path AICommand & Control High
Wire-side catch-all for hosts reaching the article's Sentry ingest domain or the project-specific `/api/4511539669368912/envelope/` path — independent of the process that initiated it (covers proxied/wrapped variants and Linux/macOS dev hosts where Cargo runs). Rationale: Article names the exact ingest hostname `o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io` and project envelope path `/api/4511539669368912/envelope/`. Domain alone is so specific that any internal DNS resolution or HTTP request to it is high-confidence — and catches process variants (the maintainer's GitHub repo is also compromised, so the payload could land via `git clone` rather than crates.io). 30-day lookback because exfil-per-commit means even one historical hit is interesting. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/cenotelie/onering/issues/1
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Project legitimately using a Sentry org with the same numeric org-id (collisions are astronomically unlikely for this specific id but technically possible)
  • Threat-intel platform proxy fetching the article or IOC bundles citing the domain
  • Detection-engineering lab host reproducing the IOC for rule tuning
  • Internal Sentry-on-prem instance whose path namespace happens to coincide (won't share the public DNS name)
  • Browser preview from analyst clicking the article URL
Response runbook
1) Triage: enrich the source host with cargo / Rust toolchain inventory and recent process tree; identify the process that owned the egress (curl vs sentry-rust SDK vs something else). 2) Contain: sinkhole `o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io` at corporate DNS and add a deny on the URL path at the egress proxy; isolate impacted hosts; treat the most recent git diff on each impacted repo as leaked and rotate any secrets it touched. 3) Hunt: dump every host that resolved the domain in the last 90 days; for each, run `cargo tree` against every repo on disk for `onering` 1.4.1; check the maintainer's GitHub repo (https://github.com/cenotelie/onering) is pinned to a vetted commit, not main.
union
(DeviceNetworkEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where RemoteUrl has "o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io" or RemoteUrl has "4511539669368912/envelope"
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort),
(DeviceEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
 | where AdditionalFields has "o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io"
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AdditionalFields)
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImWebSession
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where Url has "o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io" or Url has "4511539669368912/envelope"
 | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpMethod, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr),
(ImDnsActivity
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where DnsQuery has "o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io"
 | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName),
(CommonSecurityLog
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where RequestURL has "o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io" or RequestURL has "4511539669368912/envelope" or DestinationHostName has "o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io"
 | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, RequestURL, DestinationHostName, DestinationIP, RequestMethod)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cargo dependency manifest or download pinned to compromised onering 1.4.1 AIDelivery Medium
Catches the supply-chain ingress: file writes to Cargo.lock / Cargo.toml mentioning the malicious crate version, or HTTPS downloads of the onering 1.4.1 crate tarball from crates.io. Targets the build-time moment when a dev pulls the poisoned dependency, before build.rs runs. Rationale: Anchors on the article's explicit IOC `onering 1.4.1 from crates.io`. Cargo writes the cache file `onering-1.4.1.crate` under `~/.cargo/registry/cache/<index>/` and updates Cargo.lock with the pinned version on resolve — both are deterministic side-effects of pulling the poisoned dep. Article also flags that the GitHub repo is compromised, so we keep the file-write detection generic enough to fire on git-cloned dependencies (where the URL fetch wouldn't trigger). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/cenotelie/onering/issues/1 • https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/registries.html
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or detection engineer intentionally fetching the IOC for sandboxing
  • Mirror/proxy of crates.io pre-fetching the malicious version into local cache before a yank propagates
  • Vulnerability scanner like cargo-audit or Aikido enumerating the version
  • Legacy CI pipeline still referencing onering 1.4.1 after yank but on an isolated build agent
  • Developer cleaning up `Cargo.lock` after a known-bad pull (Cargo writes the file even on `cargo update --precise` to a safe version, with onering removed)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the host's `~/.cargo/registry/cache/**/onering-1.4.1.crate` and confirm SHA256 matches the malicious tarball; grep every repo on disk for `onering` in Cargo.lock and note the version. 2) Contain: instruct the dev to `cargo update -p onering --precise <safe-version>` or remove the dependency, force a fresh `cargo build` in a clean target dir, and on shared CI invalidate the cargo cache. 3) Hunt: across the org's source-control, run `git grep -E 'onering.*=.*"1\.4\.1"'` on every Rust repo; check internal Cargo mirrors for any hosts that pulled the bad version; coordinate with Aikido feed for org-wide blast radius.
union
(DeviceNetworkEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where RemoteUrl has "crates.io" and (RemoteUrl has "onering/1.4.1" or RemoteUrl has "onering-1.4.1.crate")
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl),
(DeviceFileEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where FileName in~ ("Cargo.lock", "Cargo.toml")
 | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cargo.exe", "cargo")
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
(DeviceFileEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where FolderPath has ".cargo\\registry\\cache" or FolderPath has ".cargo/registry/cache"
 | where FileName has "onering-1.4.1"
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256)
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImWebSession
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where Url has "crates.io" and (Url has "onering/1.4.1" or Url has "onering-1.4.1.crate")
 | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpMethod),
(ImFileEvent
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where TargetFileName in~ ("Cargo.lock", "Cargo.toml")
 | where ActingProcessName has "cargo"
 | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessCommandLine),
(ImFileEvent
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where TargetFileName has "onering-1.4.1"
 | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
(source:zeek (@http.url:*crates.io*onering\/1.4.1* OR @http.url:*crates.io*onering-1.4.1.crate*)) OR (source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:PATH @file.path:*\/.cargo\/registry\/cache\/*onering-1.4.1*) OR (source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:*\\.cargo\\registry\\cache\\*onering-1.4.1* OR @TargetFilename:*\\Cargo.lock OR @TargetFilename:*\\Cargo.toml))
(#event_simpleName=FileWritten (TargetFileName=/onering-1\.4\.1/i OR (TargetFileName=/[\\/](Cargo\.lock|Cargo\.toml)$/i ContextImageFileName=/cargo(\.exe)?$/i))) OR (#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(static\.)?crates\.io/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

Microsoft Patches Record 206 Flaws, Including Three Zero-Days and Critical RCE Bugs

The Hacker News
2026-06-10 13 use cases 4 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

Microsoft on Tuesday released fixes for a record 206 security vulnerabilities impacting its software portfolio, including three flaws that have been publicly disclosed at the time of release. Of the 206 flaws, 39 are rated Critical, and 167 are rated Important in severity. This includes 63 privilege escalation, 56 remote code execution, 30 information disclosure, 27 spoofing, 20 security

Surface hosts in the org still missing the June 2026 Patch Tuesday updates for the critical pre-auth RCEs (CVE-2026-45657 kernel TCP/IP, CVE-2026-47291 HTTP.sys, CVE-2026-44815 DHCP Client) and the publicly-disclosed zero-days (CVE-2026-45586 CTFMON, CVE-2026-49160 HTTP.sys DoS, CVE-2026-50507 BitLocker). Use Defender TVM software vulnerability data — these CVEs are all in the June 2026 KB rollup and require none of the others to be exploitable. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE list pulled out of the article body (CVE-2026-45657/47291/44815/45585/45655/45658/50507/45586/49160 plus the two non-Microsoft CVE-2025-10263 and CVE-2026-8863). TVM joins keep it to vulnerable software actually installed, not just the CVE catalogue.

Step 3: Hunt — pivot on the still-exposed devices into the other UCs in this set (HTTP.sys/DHCP child-process anomalies, MaxHeadersCount registry tampering, CTFMON LPE) to confirm none have already been exploited pre-patch.

HTTP/2 Bomb mitigation tampering — MaxHeadersCount registry value (CVE-2026-49160) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Watch for write, delete, or downward modification of the new `MaxHeadersCount` registry value under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\HTTP\Parameters. Microsoft introduced this value specifically to mitigate the HTTP/2 Bomb DoS against IIS/HTTP.sys (CVE-2026-49160). An attacker who reaches admin on an IIS host could remove or set it to 0 to re-enable the DoS surface; conversely the value going from set→unset on a host that previously had it is a tampering signal. Rationale: Pulls the exact registry path and value name (`MaxHeadersCount` under `HTTP\Parameters`) that the article quotes Microsoft as introducing in the June 2026 update. Tamper-with-the-mitigation is a higher-fidelity signal than trying to detect the HTTP/2 Bomb payload itself on the wire, which IIS logs don't expose at header-count granularity.
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1112
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin manually applying or tuning the new mitigation (legitimate IIS hardening sweep)
  • Configuration management tools (DSC / Ansible / GPO) deploying the registry value across an IIS fleet
  • Microsoft KB rollback during a problematic patch cycle
  • IIS performance team raising the limit above default for a high-header app
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("TrustedInstaller.exe","MsiExec.exe","services.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
Step 1: Triage — pull `InitiatingProcessFileName` and account; legitimate sets come from `services.exe`/`TrustedInstaller.exe` or known CM agents. Anything signed by an interactive user, cmd.exe, powershell.exe, or LOLBins is suspicious. Step 2: Contain — if change is unexpected, restore the value (>= 100 is Microsoft's default, see KB) and snapshot the IIS host. Step 3: Hunt — look back 24h on the same host for w3wp.exe spawning shells, IIS module installs (`appcmd.exe install module`), or unexpected HTTP/2 traffic spikes; pivot to the HTTP.sys/IIS anomalous-child UC.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\HTTP\Parameters"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "MaxHeadersCount"
| where ActionType in~ ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryValueDeleted","RegistryKeyDeleted")
| extend NewVal = tostring(RegistryValueData), PrevVal = tostring(PreviousRegistryValueData)
| where ActionType != "RegistryValueSet" or NewVal in ("0","0x0","") or toint(NewVal) < toint(coalesce(PrevVal,"0"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, NewVal, PrevVal,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\HTTP\Parameters"
| where RegistryValue =~ "MaxHeadersCount"
| where EventType in~ ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryValueDeleted","RegistryKeyDeleted")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData,
          RegistryPreviousValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: HTTP.sys MaxHeadersCount Mitigation Tampering (CVE-2026-49160 HTTP/2 Bomb)
id: 8d1f3a72-2a2f-4b91-9e6b-f1b3d2e4a0c7
description: Detects modification or deletion of the MaxHeadersCount registry value under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\HTTP\Parameters, which Microsoft introduced in the June 2026 patch as the mitigation for the HTTP/2 Bomb DoS (CVE-2026-49160). Removal or zeroing of this value re-enables the DoS surface against IIS / HTTP.sys.

#event_simpleName=AsepValueUpdate
| RegObjectName=/\\SYSTEM\\CurrentControlSet\\Services\\HTTP\\Parameters/i
| RegValueName=/MaxHeadersCount/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RegObjectName, RegValueName, RegStringValue, ContextImageFileName], function=count())

DHCP Client svchost anomalous child process (CVE-2026-44815 post-exploit) AIExploitation High
CVE-2026-44815 is a pre-auth stack-overflow RCE in the Windows DHCP Client. The DHCP Client service runs in svchost.exe under the `LocalServiceNetworkRestricted` host with the `Dhcp` service argument. Successful exploitation would surface as svchost (DHCP-hosted) spawning a non-svchost child — there is essentially no legitimate reason for `Dhcp`-hosted svchost to create a shell, script host, or LOLBin. Rationale: Article: 'CVE-2026-44815 ... allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network ... systems handling DHCP traffic should be treated as high-priority patch targets.' DHCP Client svchost normally never spawns shells; pairing the parent (`-s Dhcp` / `LocalServiceNetworkRestricted`) with the LocalService SID and a LOLBin child is a low-FP combination.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Microsoft DHCP troubleshooting kits running `ipconfig.exe` under the service context
  • Endpoint management agents (Intune/SCCM) invoking `net.exe` via the DHCP host briefly during network re-init
  • MDM remediation scripts that target DHCP renewal
  • Sysinternals procdump / handle.exe by IR team taking dumps of svchost
Suppression filter
| where ChildCmd !has "ipconfig /renew"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
Step 1: Triage — confirm the parent command line really contains `-s Dhcp` (not another svchost service); pull the SHA256 of the child and the network connections from the same `InitiatingProcessId` ±5 min. Step 2: Contain — isolate the host with Defender 'Isolate device' or NAC quarantine; capture the DHCP packet trace if still online (rogue DHCP server may be persistent on the LAN). Step 3: Hunt — across the same subnet, look for additional DHCP Client hosts that received a DHCP OFFER from the same MAC, and pivot to the patch-inventory UC for CVE-2026-44815 to find other still-vulnerable hosts on the same broadcast domain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("-s Dhcp", "-s dhcp", "LocalServiceNetworkRestricted")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","nltest.exe","ipconfig.exe","hostname.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, AccountDomain,
          ParentImage=InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage=FolderPath,
          ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine,
          ProcessIntegrityLevel,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\svchost.exe"
| extend NewBase = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
| where NewBase in ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","net.exe","whoami.exe","nltest.exe","ipconfig.exe")
| where SubjectUserSid in ("S-1-5-19","S-1-5-20")  // LOCAL SERVICE / NETWORK SERVICE — DHCP runs as LocalService
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType, ProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HTTP.sys / IIS w3wp.exe spawning shell or LOLBin (CVE-2026-47291 post-exploit) AIExploitation High
CVE-2026-47291 is an integer overflow in HTTP.sys (kernel) allowing unauthenticated network RCE. Post-exploitation in IIS environments typically surfaces as the w3wp.exe app-pool worker spawning cmd/powershell or LOLBins, or as `System` process anomalies. This rule pivots on the w3wp parent → suspicious child shape which is essentially absent in healthy IIS operations. Rationale: Article: 'CVE-2026-47291 ... integer overflow ... in Windows HTTP.sys that allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network.' HTTP.sys is a kernel driver, but IIS deployments funnel HTTP.sys traffic into w3wp.exe app-pool workers — successful exploitation gives the attacker code in that context. w3wp spawning cmd/PowerShell is high-fidelity (legitimate web apps rarely shell out).
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy ASP.NET apps using `Process.Start("cmd /c ...")` for legitimate batch work (e.g. PDF rendering, ImageMagick wrappers)
  • SharePoint or Exchange Health Manager scripts that invoke PowerShell from w3wp
  • WebDeploy / msdeploy.exe operations during application deploys
  • Web-based admin consoles (HelpDesk apps, ITSM portals) that legitimately invoke `net.exe`/`whoami.exe` on behalf of authenticated admins
Suppression filter
| where ChildCmd !contains "WebDeploy" and ChildCmd !contains "msdeploy"
| where ParentCmd !contains "HealthMailbox"
Response runbook
Step 1: Triage — pull the parent w3wp.exe command line to identify the IIS App Pool (`-ap` argument). Check if that pool is on a known-legacy/known-shells allowlist for the org; if not, treat as live. Step 2: Contain — recycle the App Pool, capture a memory dump of w3wp.exe via Sysinternals procdump, and isolate the host. Pull the IIS access logs for the 5 minutes prior — large or malformed POSTs to .aspx/.asmx handlers are the likely vector. Step 3: Hunt — search the IIS inetpub wwwroot folders for new .aspx/.ashx/.config files created by the IIS worker (web shells), and pivot to CVE-2026-47291 patch status across the IIS fleet.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","nltest.exe","systeminfo.exe","tasklist.exe","ipconfig.exe","hostname.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, AccountDomain,
          ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ParentIntegrity=InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel,
          ChildImage=FolderPath,
          ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine,
          ChildIntegrity=ProcessIntegrityLevel,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\w3wp.exe"
| extend NewBase = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
| where NewBase in ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","nltest.exe","systeminfo.exe","tasklist.exe","ipconfig.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, TargetUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
